title: Parity-doublet spin interactions in ultracold polyatomic molecules
authors: Junheng Tao, Paige Robichaud, Christian Hallas, Giseok Lee, John M. Doyle
abstract: Precision measurements exploit internal molecular structure to search for physics beyond the Standard Model. Reaching the entanglement-enhanced regime requires preparing and preserving correlated molecular states within the same manifold used for sensing. Parity-doublet states are central to proposals for precision measurements with polyatomic molecules because they enable large molecular polarization for enhanced sensitivity, and provide internal state co-magnetometry to suppress systematic errors. Here we report the observation and control of resonant dipolar exchange interactions in a parity-doublet sensing manifold of ultracold polyatomic molecules. Using laser-cooled CaOH molecules in a crossed optical dipole trap, we encode a pseudospin in the $\ell$-type parity-doublet states and observe two complementary signatures of interactions: a density-dependent Ramsey contrast decay and a spin-projection-dependent mean-field precession whose sign reverses with the initialized population imbalance. Both observables are well described by a common discrete truncated Wigner model using independently calibrated experimental parameters. We further Floquet-engineer the interaction anisotropy and observe suppressed many-body dephasing near the SU(2)-symmetric Heisenberg point, identifying a protected regime relevant for spin squeezing and precision measurement with dense molecular ensembles. Our results establish parity doublets as a coherent, interacting, and programmable molecular degree of freedom, connecting the polyatomic precision-measurement platform to dipolar many-body physics and opening a route to entanglement-enhanced tests of fundamental physics.
summary: This paper reports the observation and control of resonant dipolar exchange interactions in the parity-doublet states of ultracold polyatomic molecules. By measuring both coherence decay and mean-field precession, the researchers confirmed the system's utility as a programmable, interacting quantum resource. This work advances the field by linking molecular structure to many-body physics for next-generation quantum sensors.
main_problem: To establish parity-doublet states as a programmable, interacting degree of freedom in ultracold polyatomic molecules for enhanced precision measurements and tests of fundamental physics.
main_result: The authors observed resonant dipolar exchange interactions and demonstrated that the system's dynamics are governed by a controllable, interacting many-body Hamiltonian, opening a route to entanglement-enhanced metrology.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (Ramsey decay, mean-field precession) with theoretical modeling using the Discrete Truncated Wigner Approximation (DTWA) and scattering theory.
model_or_system: The system uses ultracold $	ext{CaOH}$ molecules trapped in a crossed optical dipole trap, utilizing the parity-doublet states derived from the $\ell$-type bending vibrational mode as a pseudo-spin qubit manifold.
key_observables: Density-dependent Ramsey contrast decay, spin-projection-dependent mean-field precession rate ($\omega_{mf}$), and the rate of many-body dephasing ($\Gamma$).
important_parameters: The system is characterized by the anisotropic dipole-dipole interaction strength $V(\mathbf{r})$ and the ability to tune the interaction anisotropy ($\Delta$) via Floquet engineering.
main_assumptions: The dynamics are modeled using the DTWA, and scattering calculations rely on matching logarithmic derivatives at defined inner and outer boundaries.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the geometry of the dipolar interaction, the $	ext{N}=1$ rotational state diagram, and plots showing Ramsey contrast decay versus time and density, and spin precession phase versus initial angle.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical system and the role of parity doublets, to observing complementary signatures of dipolar interactions (decay and precession), and finally to demonstrating control by engineering the interaction anisotropy to find protected, interacting regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly connects molecular quantum physics (polyatomic molecules) with fundamental many-body physics (dipolar interactions) in a highly controllable, programmable quantum platform relevant for quantum sensing.
